subject: math
title: Exponents, Roots, and Scientific Notation
objectives: Students will evaluate powers with positive, negative, and zero exponents, including powers of negative numbers.
Students will apply the product, quotient, and power rules to simplify expressions with exponents.
Students will find square roots and cube roots, estimate roots that are not whole numbers, and simplify square roots.
Students will convert between standard form and scientific notation and compute with numbers in scientific notation in real-world contexts.
Students will evaluate expressions that combine exponents, roots, and grouping symbols using the correct order of operations.
teach:
Objectives

  • Evaluate powers with positive, negative, and zero exponents, and tell the difference between (−3)2 and −32.
  • Use the product, quotient, and power rules to simplify expressions.
  • Find square roots and cube roots, estimate non-perfect roots, and simplify square roots such as √50.
  • Convert between standard form and scientific notation, and multiply and divide numbers in scientific notation (distances, populations, cell sizes).
  • Evaluate expressions with exponents and roots using the order of operations.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson and Study Sheet (the Study Sheet has the perfect squares and cubes table)
  • Scratch paper and pencils; students should write every step
  • A scientific calculator for the last ten minutes only, so students can practice the exponent, square root, and scientific notation keys
  • Optional: index cards for a quick “perfect squares” flash drill

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick problems that check what students remember about powers, roots, and order of operations.
Direct instruction20Exponents and negative bases (4 min), exponent rules including zero and negative exponents (6 min), roots and simplifying radicals (4 min), scientific notation (4 min), order of operations with exponents (2 min). Model the worked examples.
Guided practice15Students work six problems in pairs or along with you; you check each step.
Independent practice15Students start the 12 weekly practice items (items 1–8 in class; finish at home).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding, preview of the exit ticket, and this week's study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Put these on the board as students arrive. Let them know this is a quick check, not a grade.

  1. 32
  2. 23
  3. √49
  4. 103
  5. 4 + 2 × 3

Answers: (1) 9   (2) 8   (3) 7   (4) 1,000   (5) 10

Watch for students who answer 6 for problem 1 or problem 2. That is the single most common exponent error (multiplying the base by the exponent), and you will address it in the first two minutes. Problem 5 reviews Week 1: multiplication comes before addition.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. What an exponent means (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • An exponent tells how many times to use the base as a factor. In 53, the base is 5 and the exponent is 3: 53 = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. It is never 5 × 3.
  • Read 52 as “5 squared” and 53 as “5 cubed.” Any other power is “to the fourth power,” “to the fifth power,” and so on.
  • Powers of 10 are easy: the exponent tells how many zeros. 104 = 10,000.
  • Negative bases need parentheses. (−3)2 means (−3)(−3) = 9. But −32 means “the opposite of 32,” which is −9. The exponent applies only to what it touches.
  • A negative base raised to an even power is positive; raised to an odd power it is negative. This is the Week 1 sign rule: count the negative factors.

Worked Example 1 (powers and negative bases). Evaluate each expression.

(a) 25 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32

(b) (−3)2 = (−3)(−3) = 9

(c) −32 = −(3 × 3) = −9

(d) (−2)3 = (−2)(−2)(−2) = 4 × (−2) = −8

Answers: (a) 32   (b) 9   (c) −9   (d) −8. Ask the class why (b) and (c) are different. Expected: in (b) the parentheses put the negative sign inside the base; in (c) the exponent touches only the 3.

2. Exponent rules (about 6 minutes)

Talking points: Build each rule from the meaning of an exponent, so students can rebuild it on test day if they forget it.

  • Product rule: xa · xb = xa+b. Show x2 · x3 = (x · x)(x · x · x) = x5. Same base: add the exponents. Coefficients still multiply: 3x2 · 4x3 = 12x5.
  • Quotient rule: xa ÷ xb = xa−b. Show x5 ÷ x2: two pairs of x cancel, leaving x3. Same base: subtract the exponents.
  • Power rule: (xa)b = xab. Show (x2)3 = x2 · x2 · x2 = x6. A power of a power: multiply the exponents. A power of a product applies to every factor: (2x3)2 = 22x6 = 4x6.
  • Zero exponent: any nonzero number to the zero power is 1. Show the pattern 23 = 8, 22 = 4, 21 = 2, 20 = 1 (each step divides by 2). Or: x4 ÷ x4 = x0, and anything divided by itself is 1.
  • Negative exponent: keep the pattern going: 2−1 = 1/2, 2−2 = 1/4, 2−3 = 1/8. In general x−n = 1/xn. A negative exponent means “reciprocal,” not “negative number.”
  • The rules only work when the bases are the same. 23 · 32 cannot be combined into one power; just evaluate: 8 × 9 = 72.

Worked Example 2 (exponent rules).

(a) Simplify (2x3)2 · x−4.

Power rule on every factor: (2x3)2 = 22 · x3×2 = 4x6

Product rule: 4x6 · x−4 = 4x6+(−4) = 4x2

(b) Evaluate 5−2.

5−2 = 1/52 = 1/25

(c) Evaluate 37 ÷ 35.

Quotient rule: 37−5 = 32 = 9

Answers: (a) 4x2   (b) 1/25   (c) 9. For (a), the most common wrong answer is 2x6 · x−4 = 2x2 (forgetting to square the 2). For (b), the most common wrong answer is −10 or −25.

3. Square roots, cube roots, and simplifying radicals (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A square root undoes squaring: √49 = 7 because 72 = 49. On the GED, √ means the positive (principal) root.
  • A cube root undoes cubing: ∛125 = 5 because 53 = 125. Cube roots of negative numbers are allowed: ∛(−8) = −2 because (−2)3 = −8. The square root of a negative number is not a real number.
  • Estimating: √40 is between √36 = 6 and √49 = 7, and closer to 6. A calculator gives about 6.32.
  • Simplifying: look for the largest perfect-square factor. √50 = √(25 × 2) = √25 × √2 = 5√2.
  • You can split a root across multiplication, but never across addition: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5, not 3 + 4 = 7.

Worked Example 3 (roots).

(a) ∛64: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so ∛64 = 4

(b) Simplify √48. Perfect-square factors of 48: 4 and 16. Use the largest, 16.

√48 = √(16 × 3) = √16 × √3 = 4√3

Check: (4√3)2 = 16 × 3 = 48. Correct.

(c) Between which two whole numbers is √90? 92 = 81 and 102 = 100, and 81 < 90 < 100, so √90 is between 9 and 10.

Answers: (a) 4   (b) 4√3   (c) between 9 and 10. If a student uses 4 instead of 16 in (b), they get 2√12, which is correct in value but not fully simplified because 12 still has the factor 4.

4. Scientific notation (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10n, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. Scientists use it for very large numbers (distances in space, populations) and very small numbers (the size of cells and bacteria).
  • Standard form to scientific notation: move the decimal point until exactly one nonzero digit is to its left. Count the moves. Big number: positive exponent. Small number (less than 1): negative exponent.
  • Examples: 384,000 km (about the distance from Earth to the Moon) = 3.84 × 105 km. A red blood cell is about 0.0000075 m wide = 7.5 × 10−6 m.
  • Multiplying: multiply the front numbers, add the exponents, then adjust so the front number is between 1 and 10.
  • Dividing: divide the front numbers, subtract the exponents, then adjust.
  • Compare numbers in scientific notation by looking at the exponent first; if the exponents match, compare the front numbers.

Worked Example 4 (scientific notation with populations). The world population is about 8 × 109 people. A large city has about 4 × 106 people. About how many times greater is the world population than the city's population?

Divide: (8 × 109) ÷ (4 × 106)

Front numbers: 8 ÷ 4 = 2

Powers of 10: 109 ÷ 106 = 109−6 = 103

Result: 2 × 103 = 2,000

Answer: about 2,000 times greater.

Follow-up (multiplying and adjusting): (6 × 104)(5 × 103) = 30 × 107. The front number 30 is not between 1 and 10, so rewrite 30 as 3 × 101: 3 × 101 × 107 = 3 × 108.

5. Order of operations with exponents and roots (about 2 minutes)

Talking points: Exponents and roots come right after grouping symbols. A root symbol is also a grouping symbol: work everything under it first. Rewrite the whole expression after each step.

Worked Example 5 (order of operations). Evaluate 4 + 3(23 − 5)2 ÷ 9 − √16.

Inside the parentheses, the exponent first: 23 = 8, then 8 − 5 = 3. Expression: 4 + 3(3)2 ÷ 9 − √16

Exponents and roots: 32 = 9 and √16 = 4. Expression: 4 + 3 × 9 ÷ 9 − 4

Multiply and divide left to right: 3 × 9 = 27; 27 ÷ 9 = 3. Expression: 4 + 3 − 4

Add and subtract left to right: 4 + 3 = 7; 7 − 4 = 3

Answer: 3. The common wrong path is computing 3 × 3 = 9 before squaring, which gives (9)2 = 81 and a final answer of 9.

Teacher note: If time is short, model Examples 2, 4, and 5 fully and assign Example 3 as a think-aloud for a volunteer. Keep calculators away until the last ten minutes. The first part of the GED math test does not allow a calculator, and exponent rules, perfect squares, and simple roots are ideal no-calculator questions.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Give students about two minutes per problem, then have a volunteer explain each step aloud while you write it.

  1. Write 24 · 23 as a single power of 2, then find its value.
  2. Evaluate (−5)2 and −52.
  3. Evaluate 6−2.
  4. Simplify √75.
  5. Write 0.00062 in scientific notation.
  6. Evaluate 18 − (1 + 2)2 × 2 + ∛8.

Answers with steps:

1. Same base, add exponents: 24+3 = 27 = 128.

2. (−5)2 = (−5)(−5) = 25; −52 = −(5 × 5) = −25.

3. 6−2 = 1/62 = 1/36.

4. Largest perfect-square factor of 75 is 25: √75 = √(25 × 3) = 5√3.

5. Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 6.2. The number is less than 1, so the exponent is negative: 6.2 × 10−4.

6. Parentheses: 1 + 2 = 3. Exponents and roots: 32 = 9 and ∛8 = 2. Expression: 18 − 9 × 2 + 2. Multiply: 9 × 2 = 18. Then 18 − 18 + 2 = 2.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students open this week's 12 practice items and complete items 1–8 in class. Items 9–12 are the harder multi-step problems; students finish them at home. Look at scratch work, not just answers. When a student is stuck, ask “What does the exponent tell you to do?” or “Are the bases the same?” before giving a hint. Let students use a calculator for the last few minutes on item 11 only, and show them where the exponent and scientific notation keys are.

Checks for Understanding

  • Is 23 equal to 6? Expected: No. 23 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
  • What is 10−3 as a decimal? Expected: 0.001 (1/1,000).
  • Write 40,000 in scientific notation. Expected: 4 × 104.
  • Why is 25 × 103 not in scientific notation? Expected: the front number must be at least 1 and less than 10. The correct form is 2.5 × 104.
  • √50 is between which two whole numbers? Expected: 7 and 8, because 49 < 50 < 64.
  • What is any nonzero number to the zero power? Expected: 1.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Multiplying the base by the exponent. Students write 43 = 12. Correction: have them write the repeated multiplication every time until it is automatic: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

Ignoring parentheses on a negative base. Students say −62 = 36. Correction: ask “What does the exponent touch?” Without parentheses it touches only the 6, so −62 = −36. With parentheses, (−6)2 = 36.

Treating a negative exponent as a negative number. Students say 2−3 = −8 or −6. Correction: return to the pattern 21 = 2, 20 = 1, 2−1 = 1/2, 2−2 = 1/4, 2−3 = 1/8. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, and the value is still positive.

Mixing up the rules. Students multiply exponents in x2 · x3 (getting x6) or add them in (x2)3 (getting x5). Correction: write both out the long way side by side. Multiplying powers adds exponents; a power of a power multiplies them.

Combining different bases or adding powers. Students write 23 · 32 = 65, or 23 + 22 = 25. Correction: the rules need the same base and multiplication or division. Evaluate instead: 8 × 9 = 72 and 8 + 4 = 12.

Splitting a root across addition. Students write √(9 + 16) = 3 + 4 = 7. Correction: the root bar is a grouping symbol. Add first: √25 = 5.

Moving the decimal the wrong way in scientific notation. Students write 0.0045 = 4.5 × 103. Correction: ask “Is the number bigger or smaller than 1?” Small numbers get negative exponents: 4.5 × 10−3. Check by moving the decimal back.

Differentiation

Support: Give students the perfect squares and cubes table from the Study Sheet during practice. Have them expand every power the long way before using a rule, and write each rule on an index card with one example. For scientific notation, use a place-value chart and physically move a paper “decimal point” while counting. Break order-of-operations problems into one step per line.

Stretch: Offer expressions that combine several rules, such as (3x2y)3 ÷ (9x4y2). Steps: (3x2y)3 = 27x6y3; 27 ÷ 9 = 3; x6−4 = x2; y3−2 = y. Answer: 3x2y. Also ask: light travels about 3 × 105 km per second; how far does it travel in one minute? (3 × 105 × 60 = 180 × 105 = 1.8 × 107 km.)

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Ask two or three of the checks for understanding. Have each student state one rule they will remember (for example, “same base, multiplying: add the exponents”). Preview the Post Lesson exit ticket and this week's study plan, including this week's Practice GED.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • No-calculator questions. The short first part of the math test often includes evaluating a power, a perfect square root, or simplifying with exponent rules. Students should know the perfect squares through 152 and the cubes through 53 by heart.
  • Calculator questions. The on-screen scientific calculator has keys for squaring, powers, square roots, and scientific notation. Students should still estimate first so they can catch a typing error.
  • Question formats. Multiple choice (“Which expression is equivalent to…”), fill-in-the-blank (type a number or a value in standard form), drop-down menus (choose the simplified power), and drag-and-drop (order numbers written in scientific notation).
  • Typical wording. “Which expression is equivalent to (x4)3?” “What is the value of the expression?” “Which number is written in scientific notation?” “How many times greater is…?” “Between which two consecutive whole numbers is √55?”
  • Built-in traps. Wrong answer choices come from the mistakes above: base times exponent, negative exponent read as a negative number, adding exponents when they should be multiplied, and decimal moves in the wrong direction. Remind students that seeing their answer in the list does not prove it is right.
  • Connections. Exponents return in Week 6 (area and volume formulas use squares and cubes), Week 7 (polynomials), and Week 10 (quadratics). The Pythagorean theorem in Week 5 depends on square roots.
student:
Welcome to Week 3

This week you will learn the shorthand that mathematicians and scientists use for repeated multiplication, how to undo it with roots, and how to write very large and very small numbers in a compact way. These skills show up often on the GED, sometimes in the part of the test where you cannot use a calculator. Read each section, study the examples, and write every step on paper.

1. What an Exponent Means

An exponent tells you how many times to multiply a number, called the base, by itself.

Key idea: 43 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. The base is 4 and the exponent is 3. It does not mean 4 × 3.

  • x2 is read “x squared.” x3 is read “x cubed.”
  • Powers of 10: the exponent tells how many zeros. 105 = 100,000.
  • Negative bases: the exponent applies only to what it touches. (−2)4 = (−2)(−2)(−2)(−2) = 16, but −24 = −(2 × 2 × 2 × 2) = −16.

Example 1. Evaluate (a) 34   (b) (−4)3   (c) −42

(a) 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 9 × 9 = 81

(b) (−4)(−4)(−4) = 16 × (−4) = −64

(c) The exponent touches only the 4: −(4 × 4) = −16

Answers: (a) 81   (b) −64   (c) −16

2. Exponent Rules

These rules work when the bases are the same.

RuleWhat to doExample
Product rule: xa · xb = xa+bMultiplying: add the exponentsx5 · x2 = x7
Quotient rule: xa ÷ xb = xa−bDividing: subtract the exponentsy8 ÷ y3 = y5
Power rule: (xa)b = xabPower of a power: multiply the exponents(a4)3 = a12
Zero exponent: x0 = 1Any nonzero number to the 0 power is 160 = 1
Negative exponent: x−n = 1/xnTake the reciprocal3−2 = 1/32 = 1/9

Why does x5 · x2 = x7? Because you have five x's multiplied by two more x's, which is seven x's in all. If you ever forget a rule, write the powers out the long way and count.

Watch out: A negative exponent does not make a number negative. 2−3 = 1/8, not −8. Also, numbers in front (coefficients) still multiply: 2x3 · 5x4 = 10x7.

Example 2. Simplify (a) 4a3 · 3a5   (b) (x2)4 ÷ x3   (c) 10−2

(a) Multiply the coefficients: 4 × 3 = 12. Add the exponents: 3 + 5 = 8. Answer: 12a8

(b) Power rule: (x2)4 = x8. Quotient rule: x8 ÷ x3 = x5. Answer: x5

(c) 10−2 = 1/102 = 1/100 = 0.01

Answers: (a) 12a8   (b) x5   (c) 0.01

3. Square Roots and Cube Roots

A square root undoes squaring. √64 = 8 because 82 = 64. A cube root undoes cubing. ∛27 = 3 because 33 = 27. A cube root of a negative number is negative: ∛(−27) = −3.

Numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100 are perfect squares because their square roots are whole numbers. Learn them; they save time.

Estimating a root: √30 is not a whole number. Since 25 < 30 < 36, √30 is between 5 and 6.

Simplifying a square root: find the largest perfect square that divides the number, and take its root out front.

Example 3. (a) ∛8   (b) Simplify √45   (c) Between which two whole numbers is √70?

(a) 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, so ∛8 = 2

(b) 45 = 9 × 5, and 9 is a perfect square. √45 = √9 × √5 = 3√5

(c) 82 = 64 and 92 = 81. Since 64 < 70 < 81, √70 is between 8 and 9.

Answers: (a) 2   (b) 3√5   (c) between 8 and 9

Watch out: You cannot split a square root over addition. √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10, not 6 + 8 = 14.

4. Scientific Notation

Scientists write very large and very small numbers in scientific notation: a number at least 1 and less than 10, times a power of 10.

Steps to write a number in scientific notation:

  1. Move the decimal point so there is exactly one nonzero digit to its left.
  2. Count how many places you moved it. That is the exponent.
  3. If the original number is 10 or more, the exponent is positive. If it is less than 1, the exponent is negative.
  • Earth is about 93,000,000 miles from the Sun: 9.3 × 107 miles (the decimal moved 7 places).
  • A small bacterium is about 0.000002 meters long: 2 × 10−6 meters (the decimal moved 6 places).

To go back to standard form, move the decimal point the other way: right for a positive exponent, left for a negative exponent.

Multiplying and dividing: work with the front numbers and the powers of 10 separately, then make sure the front number is between 1 and 10.

Example 4. Find (3 × 104)(5 × 106). Write the answer in scientific notation.

Front numbers: 3 × 5 = 15

Powers of 10: 104 × 106 = 1010

So far: 15 × 1010. But 15 is not less than 10.

Rewrite 15 as 1.5 × 101: 1.5 × 101 × 1010 = 1.5 × 1011

Answer: 1.5 × 1011

Strategy: To compare numbers in scientific notation, look at the exponents first. 2 × 105 is greater than 9 × 104, even though 9 is bigger than 2, because 200,000 > 90,000.

5. Order of Operations with Exponents

Here is the full order you started in Week 1:

  1. Grouping symbols: ( ), [ ], | |, and everything under a root symbol
  2. Exponents and roots
  3. Multiplication and division, left to right
  4. Addition and subtraction, left to right

Example 5. Evaluate 20 − 2 × 32 + √25.

Exponents and roots: 32 = 9 and √25 = 5. Expression: 20 − 2 × 9 + 5

Multiply: 2 × 9 = 18. Expression: 20 − 18 + 5

Left to right: 20 − 18 = 2; 2 + 5 = 7

Answer: 7. If you multiply 2 × 3 first and then square, you get 36 and the wrong answer.

Try It

Work each problem on paper, then check your answer.

1. Evaluate (a) 53   (b) (−4)2   (c) −42

Show answer

(a) 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. (b) (−4)(−4) = 16. (c) −(4 × 4) = −16.

2. Simplify (y3)4 ÷ y5.

Show answer

Power rule: (y3)4 = y12. Quotient rule: y12−5 = y7.

3. Simplify √98.

Show answer

98 = 49 × 2, and 49 is a perfect square. √98 = √49 × √2 = 7√2.

4. Write 0.00045 in scientific notation.

Show answer

Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 4.5. The number is less than 1, so the exponent is negative: 4.5 × 10−4.

5. Evaluate 2 + 62 ÷ 4 × 3.

Show answer

Exponent: 62 = 36. Divide and multiply left to right: 36 ÷ 4 = 9; 9 × 3 = 27. Add: 2 + 27 = 29.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • An exponent tells how many times to use the base as a factor: 43 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, not 12.
  • Parentheses matter with negative bases: (−3)2 = 9, but −32 = −9.
  • Same base: multiplying adds exponents, dividing subtracts exponents, and a power of a power multiplies exponents.
  • Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1. A negative exponent means take the reciprocal: x−n = 1/xn.
  • Square roots undo squaring and cube roots undo cubing. Simplify a square root by taking out the largest perfect-square factor: √50 = 5√2.
  • Scientific notation is a × 10n with 1 ≤ a < 10. Large numbers have positive exponents; numbers less than 1 have negative exponents.
  • To multiply or divide in scientific notation, handle the front numbers and the powers of 10 separately, then adjust the front number.
  • Order of operations: grouping symbols, exponents and roots, multiplication and division left to right, addition and subtraction left to right.

Exit Ticket

1. Evaluate 34.

Show answer

3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81

2. Simplify x7 ÷ x2.

Show answer

Same base, dividing: subtract exponents. x7−2 = x5

3. Evaluate 4−1.

Show answer

4−1 = 1/41 = 1/4 (or 0.25)

4. Write 6.4 × 105 in standard form.

Show answer

Move the decimal point 5 places right: 640,000

5. Evaluate 10 − 23 + √9.

Show answer

23 = 8 and √9 = 3. Then 10 − 8 + 3 = 5.

Reflection

  • Which exponent rule is easiest for you to remember, and which one do you mix up? Write an example of each the long way.
  • Look at a problem you got wrong this week. Was the mistake about the meaning of an exponent, a rule, a root, or the direction of the decimal point?
  • Where have you seen very large or very small numbers in daily life or the news (populations, distances, budgets, germs)? How could scientific notation help you read them?

This Week's Study Plan

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread sections 1 and 2 of the Student Lesson. Redo Examples 1 and 2 without looking, then check. Make an index card for each exponent rule.20–30 min
Day 2Reread sections 3 through 5. Memorize the perfect squares through 152 and the cubes through 53. Rework the Try It problems.25–30 min
Day 3Complete all 12 weekly practice items. Read every explanation, even for the items you got right.30–40 min
Day 4Study the vocabulary and the Study Sheet. Find three large or small numbers in a news article or science website and write them in scientific notation.20–30 min
Day 5Redo any practice items you missed. Practice the exponent, square root, and scientific notation keys on a scientific calculator.20–30 min
Day 6Take this week's Practice GED for Mathematical Reasoning under timed conditions. Set aside about two hours in a quiet place.About 2 hours
Day 7Review your Practice GED results. Mark which missed questions used this week's skills and redo them.20–30 min

Test-taking strategy: test an equivalent-expression question with a small number. When the GED asks “Which expression is equivalent to (x3)2?” and you are unsure of the rule, pick x = 2. Then (23)2 = 82 = 64. Now test the choices: 26 = 64 works, but 25 = 32 does not. Plugging in a number turns a rule you might forget into arithmetic you can check.

Perfect Squares and Cubes

Scientific Notation: a × 10n, 1 ≤ a < 10

  • Big number: positive exponent. 93,000,000 = 9.3 × 107
  • Small number: negative exponent. 0.000002 = 2 × 10−6
  • To standard form: move the decimal right (+) or left (−).
  • Compare: exponent first, then front number.

Computing in Scientific Notation

  • Multiply: multiply fronts, add exponents. (3 × 104)(5 × 106) = 15 × 1010 = 1.5 × 1011
  • Divide: divide fronts, subtract exponents. (8 × 109) ÷ (4 × 106) = 2 × 103
  • Adjust so the front number is from 1 up to (not including) 10.

Top mistakes: 43 is 64, not 12; 2−3 is 1/8, not −8; multiplying powers adds exponents, a power of a power multiplies them; rules need the same base; small numbers get negative exponents.

items.hint: The exponent tells how many 2s to multiply together.
items.explain:
25 means five 2s multiplied together:

2 × 2 = 4

4 × 2 = 8

8 × 2 = 16

16 × 2 = 32

The choice 10 comes from multiplying the base by the exponent (2 × 5). The choice 25 comes from switching the base and exponent (52). The choice 7 comes from adding 2 + 5.

items.prompt:
What is the value of the expression below?

√81 + ∛27
items.hint: Which number times itself is 81? Which number used as a factor three times is 27?
items.explain:
√81 = 9 because 9 × 9 = 81.

∛27 = 3 because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.

9 + 3 = 12

The choice 18 comes from treating the cube root as dividing by 3 (27 ÷ 3 = 9, then 9 + 9). The choice 108 comes from adding 81 + 27 and ignoring the roots. The choice 49.5 comes from dividing by 2 and by 3 (40.5 + 9) instead of taking roots.

items.prompt:
The population of a small city is about 5.2 × 104 people.

Write this number in standard form.
items.hint: A positive exponent of 4 means move the decimal point 4 places to the right.
items.explain:
104 = 10,000, so 5.2 × 104 = 5.2 × 10,000.

Move the decimal point in 5.2 four places to the right, filling empty places with zeros:

5.2 → 52. → 520. → 5,200. → 52,000.

The population is 52,000 people.

A common mistake is to write 5.20000 or 520,000 by adding four zeros after the 2 instead of moving the decimal point four places.

items.hint: Exponents come before multiplication, and multiplication comes before addition.
items.explain:
Exponent first: 42 = 16. The expression is 3 + 2 × 16.

Multiply next: 2 × 16 = 32. The expression is 3 + 32.

Add: 3 + 32 = 35

The choice 80 comes from adding first: (3 + 2) × 16. The choice 67 comes from multiplying before squaring: 3 + (2 × 4)2 = 3 + 64. The choice 19 comes from treating 42 as 4 × 2 = 8.

items.hint: Multiply the numbers in front. For the same base, add the exponents.
items.explain:
Multiply the coefficients: 3 × 2 = 6.

Multiply the powers of x. The bases are the same, so add the exponents: x4 · x3 = x4+3 = x7.

The product is 6x7.

Check with x = 1: 3(1) · 2(1) = 6, and 6(1)7 = 6. Check with x = 2: 3(16) · 2(8) = 48 × 16 = 768, and 6(27) = 6 × 128 = 768.

The choice 6x12 comes from multiplying the exponents instead of adding them. The choices with 5 come from adding the coefficients instead of multiplying.

items.prompt:
Choose the expression or number that makes each statement true. Assume x ≠ 0.

x9 ÷ x3 = {{0}}

(x2)5 = {{1}}

70 = {{2}}
items.hint: Dividing powers with the same base: subtract exponents. A power of a power: multiply exponents. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1.
items.explain:
First statement: same base, dividing, so subtract the exponents: x9−3 = x6. (x3 comes from dividing 9 by 3 instead of subtracting.)

Second statement: a power of a power, so multiply the exponents: x2×5 = x10. (x7 comes from adding instead of multiplying.)

Third statement: any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, so 70 = 1. You can see why with the quotient rule: 70 = 72 ÷ 72 = 49 ÷ 49 = 1. Choosing 0 is the most common mistake.

items.hint: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal of the positive power.
items.explain:
A negative exponent means the reciprocal of the positive power:

2−3 = 1/23

23 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8

So 2−3 = 1/8

The choice −8 comes from treating the negative exponent as a negative sign on the answer. The choice −6 comes from multiplying 2 × (−3). The choice 1/6 takes the reciprocal correctly but multiplies 2 × 3 instead of finding 23.

items.prompt: The approximate widths of four cells are listed below, in meters. Drag each cell into its position so the cells are in order from smallest (1st) to largest (4th).
items.hint: Compare the exponents first. With negative exponents, the more negative the exponent, the smaller the number. If two exponents match, compare the front numbers.
items.explain:
Compare the exponents first. A more negative exponent means a smaller number: 10−6 < 10−5 < 10−4.

Two cells have the exponent −6. Compare the front numbers: 2 < 8, so the E. coli bacterium (2 × 10−6) is smaller than the red blood cell (8 × 10−6).

In standard form: 0.000002 < 0.000008 < 0.00003 < 0.00012.

Order: E. coli bacterium, red blood cell, skin cell, human egg cell.

A common mistake is to put the red blood cell last because 8 is the biggest front number. The exponent matters more than the front number.

items.hint: Find the largest perfect square that divides 72.
items.explain:
Look for the largest perfect square that is a factor of 72. The perfect squares 4, 9, and 36 all divide 72; the largest is 36.

72 = 36 × 2

√72 = √36 × √2 = 6√2

Check: (6√2)2 = 36 × 2 = 72.

The choice 36√2 moves 36 outside without taking its square root; (36√2)2 = 2,592. The choice 9√8 makes the same mistake with 9; (9√8)2 = 648. The choice 2√6 squares to only 24.

items.hint: Evaluate each one. A negative exponent gives a reciprocal; a zero exponent gives 1.
items.explain:
Evaluate each expression:

  • 4−2 = 1/42 = 1/16 Correct
  • 2−4 = 1/24 = 1/16 Correct
  • (−4)2 = (−4)(−4) = 16
  • −42 = −(4 × 4) = −16
  • 160 = 1
  • 8−2 = 1/82 = 1/64

The two expressions equal to 1/16 are 4−2 and 2−4.

−42 and (−4)2 are tempting because they use the digits 4 and 2, but neither has a negative exponent, so neither produces a reciprocal: they equal −16 and 16, not 1/16. Remember that a negative exponent means a reciprocal, and a negative sign on the base is a different thing.

items.prompt:
The distance from the Sun to Earth is about 1.5 × 108 kilometers. Light travels about 3.0 × 105 kilometers per second.

About how many seconds does it take light from the Sun to reach Earth?
items.hint: Time = distance ÷ speed. Divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents. Then make sure the front number is between 1 and 10.
items.explain:
Time = distance ÷ speed = (1.5 × 108) ÷ (3.0 × 105)

Divide the front numbers: 1.5 ÷ 3.0 = 0.5

Subtract the exponents: 108 ÷ 105 = 108−5 = 103

So far: 0.5 × 103. The front number 0.5 is less than 1, so rewrite 0.5 as 5 × 10−1:

5 × 10−1 × 103 = 5.0 × 102 seconds (500 seconds, a little over 8 minutes).

The choice 5.0 × 103 changes 0.5 to 5.0 without adjusting the exponent. The choice 2.0 × 10−3 divides speed by distance. The choice 4.5 × 1013 multiplies instead of dividing.

items.skill: Order of operations with exponents and roots
items.prompt:
Simplify the expression completely. Enter your answer as a single integer.

52 − 2(3 − 7)2 ÷ 8 + ∛(−64)
items.hint: Start inside the parentheses. Then do all exponents and roots. The cube root of a negative number is negative.
items.explain:
Parentheses first: 3 − 7 = −4. The expression is 52 − 2(−4)2 ÷ 8 + ∛(−64)

Exponents and roots:

52 = 25

(−4)2 = (−4)(−4) = 16

∛(−64) = −4, because (−4)(−4)(−4) = −64

The expression is 25 − 2 × 16 ÷ 8 + (−4)

Multiply and divide left to right: 2 × 16 = 32; 32 ÷ 8 = 4. The expression is 25 − 4 + (−4)

Add and subtract left to right: 25 − 4 = 21; 21 + (−4) = 17

A common mistake is multiplying 2 × (−4) = −8 before squaring, which gives 64 ÷ 8 = 8 and a final answer of 13. Another is taking ∛(−64) as 4, which gives 25.
